splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires all actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. The outcome affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be determined by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to find violations and revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that courts lack authority to toll supervised release terms absent explicit statutory authorization, and the term expires as specified in the judgment regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar in § 2244(b)(1) on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions; federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election rules, such as ballot-receipt deadlines. The outcome could reshape how courts evaluate candidate standing in election cases and affect challenges to mail-in voting and election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules that allegedly dilute their votes or alter election procedures before an election takes place.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing for pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules because they cannot demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity should prevail over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held that deference trumps lenity. The issue has gained significance after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines enhancements in criminal sentencing.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (requiring only one).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) or whether possessing any one is disqualifying. The split creates significant sentencing disparities, with identically situated defendants receiving different sentences depending on where they are prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as effectively meaning 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses deserves controlling deference. Some circuits continue to defer to the commentary, while others have held the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, making deference inappropriate.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses is a reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary impermissibly expands the definition beyond its plain meaning, so deference is inappropriate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), may constitute 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can serve as a basis for compassionate release, either alone or in combination with other factors. Some circuits categorically bar consideration of non-retroactive legal changes, while others allow courts to consider them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to address this but has itself provoked further disagreement about the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, either alone or in combination with other factors.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule includes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to be federally controlled. Some circuits hold the definition encompasses any state drug offense regardless of federal scheduling, while others require the substance to be on federal schedules. The Supreme Court's decision in Brown v. United States addressed the career-offender context but the issue persists in other Guidelines applications.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally controlled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal limitation.

positions.label: Federal scheduling required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value during a Chapter 13 case inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor upon good-faith conversion to Chapter 7. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have reached the opposite conclusion. This split affects debtors' incentives to convert and creditors' recovery in bankruptcy.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a), post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A)'s structure, legislative history, and policy, post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtors, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or execution of their confinement exclusively through habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241), or whether they may also pursue claims through a Bivens action or other civil remedy.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for challenges by federal prisoners to conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the execution of their sentences. Some circuits require habeas for any claim touching on the fact or duration of confinement, while others allow civil rights or other civil claims. The Eighth Circuit's opinion in Fortner v. Eischen highlights this unresolved conflict.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration-of-confinement claims
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy when a prisoner challenges the fact or duration of confinement, including BOP decisions about sentence execution like First Step Act time credits.

positions.label: Civil rights claims also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or Bivens claims to challenge conditions or execution of confinement that do not necessarily seek release from custody, even if habeas is also available.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly consider punishment as a purpose when revoking supervised release and imposing a revocation sentence, or whether revocation sentences may only serve deterrence, incapacitation, and rehabilitation.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit's en banc dissents in United States v. Esteras highlight a split on whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to punish, placing it 'at the extreme of a circuit split,' while other circuits limit revocation sentences to non-punitive purposes consistent with the policy statement in U.S.S.G. § 7B1.1.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly consider punishment as a purpose when imposing a sentence upon revocation of supervised release.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that the primary purpose of revocation is not to punish for the violation but rather to sanction the breach of trust and address the defendant's conduct going forward, limiting sentences to deterrence, incapacitation, and rehabilitation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil deadline (30 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)) or the criminal deadline (14 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in a criminal case is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of determining the applicable appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the fees motion is ancillary to the criminal case, but a minority of circuits apply the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fees motion arises out of the criminal case and is governed by the shorter criminal appeal deadline.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Post-Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal ban on firearm possession by unlawful drug users passes constitutional muster under the Second Amendment's historical-tradition test. Some circuits have upheld § 922(g)(3) as consistent with historical traditions of disarming dangerous persons, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of disarming those who pose a danger to themselves or others, and survives Second Amendment scrutiny even as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government cannot identify a sufficient historical tradition of disarming persons solely for drug use.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which bars states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any motor carrier,' extends to preempt common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for their selection or oversight of motor carriers. The split has significant implications for accident victims' ability to recover against brokers.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are 'related to' the brokers' services and therefore preempted by the FAAAA's preemption provision.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted because the safety exception or because such claims do not implicate the broker's 'services' within the meaning of the FAAAA.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal standards governing discrimination claims in hospitality and business contexts, indicating the Court found the approach sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review and suggesting a circuit split on the applicable standards.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied its own framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality establishments, which the Supreme Court found warranted review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different or conflicting standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the split that prompted certiorari.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether legal errors or constitutional claims that could have been raised in a § 2255 habeas petition may also serve as the basis for compassionate release. Some circuits permit courts to consider such claims as one factor, while others hold that compassionate release cannot be used as a substitute for habeas review.

positions.label: May consider conviction-related errors
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A) may not be used as a vehicle to challenge the validity of a conviction or sentence, as those claims must be raised through § 2255 habeas proceedings.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
